extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature; literary critics and general educated readers interested in evaluating poetry and education
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for judging poetry and prose (qualities of 'fit' prose, what makes a poem 'classic'), plus principles about what counts as culture and how education should balance letters and sciences. Applicable to critics, students, and readers forming serious estimates of literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit prose qualities: regularity, uniformity, precision, balance
rubrics_metrics.description: "The needful qualities for a fit prose are regularity, uniformity, precision, balance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the qualities required for a 'fit' prose suitable to an age of prose and reason; writers who set out to establish such prose must give predominating attention to them. Warning: an almost exclusive attention to these qualities "involves some repression and silencing of poetry" — i.e., trade-offs exist between prose fitness and poetic freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic criticism of life (scope and seriousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should proceed from "an adequate poetic criticism of life" — having "a high seriousness, or even... poetic largeness, freedom, insight, benignity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a poet's work exhibits a comprehensive, serious, and large-minded critique of life rather than merely polished versification. Dryden and Pope may be technically admirable yet lack this deeper critical seriousness, making them 'classics of our prose' rather than of our poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: High seriousness born of absolute sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: The accent of "high seriousness, born of absolute sincerity," is essential to the power of great poetic criticism of life (Arnold invokes Dante as example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuine poetic solemnity from mere preaching or moralizing. Passages that feel like sermonizing or bravado lack the inward sincerity required for the highest poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of ideas to life under poetic truth and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The "application of ideas to life" in verse must be made "under the conditions fixed by the laws of poetic truth and poetic beauty."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A powerful idea applied to life does not by itself make great poetry; assess whether the application conforms to poetic laws (truth of feeling, tone, form). Burns sometimes applies ideas powerfully but, at times, fails to meet these poetic conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of matter and truth of manner
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's work should have both "truth of matter and truth of manner" — substance and a corresponding authentic style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this double-test to judge soundness: truthful subject-matter (insight, observation) paired with a manner (language, form) that honestly and aptly renders it. Arnold cites Burns as having these qualities frequently, which makes his poetry 'sound to the core.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Accent of poetic voice vs. bravado or inauthentic tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should convey the "accent of sincerity" — not bravado or an affected persona; otherwise the speaker does not appear to be 'the man speaking to us with his real voice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for inauthentic or performative tones (e.g., bacchanalian bravado without sincerity) as anti-patterns that undercut poetic authority and seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to triumph over an unattractive or sordid world
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may work in an unattractive world (harsh, sordid, repulsive), yet achieve supreme poetic success if the poet's genius 'triumphs over his world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the poet's truth, largeness, and manner can transcend an unpleasant milieu (examples: Burns' 'Tam o' Shanter' and 'The Jolly Beggars' as poems that triumph despite sordid content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner/influence: catching a poetic point of view (classical/Greek disposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic manner and point of view can be inherited or 'caught' from earlier masters (e.g., Gray caught the Greek poetic point of view and manner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a poet's intellectual and artistic sources and whether they acquire and employ a coherent, classical point of view or manner; possession of such manner can make an otherwise limited poet 'classic' in certain respects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of great classic poets as touchstones to correct personal/national bias
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid misleading personal or national estimates, compare contemporary poets to the work of the great classics as a touchstone for real evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly correct for personal partiality by measuring poets against the seriousness, largeness, and virtue of the great classics; Arnold applies this method to correct historic and personal biases in appraising Burns, Shelley, Byron, Wordsworth, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness and wholesomeness (perfection of soundness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain poems exhibit a 'perfection of soundness' — wholesome, solid poetic workmanship that makes them salutary and valuable (contrast with overly idealized, decorative poetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value poems that are sturdy and sound (clear truth of matter and manner), especially as a corrective to overly aestheticized or sentimental poets; Arnold praises Burns' arch, lighter pieces as particularly wholesome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the best which has been thought and said in the world
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture aims 'to know ourselves and the world' by knowing 'the best which has been thought and said in the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cultured education should acquaint learners with the most significant intellectual and artistic products across antiquity and modern times — not limited to decorative 'belles lettres' but inclusive of works that shape thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine humanism as scientific study of original sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Wolf: 'All learning is scientific which is systematically laid out and followed up to its original sources.' Genuine humanism means studying classical remains correctly in the original languages and with systematic method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate literary/humanistic study by its rigor and fidelity to primary sources; avoid a merely superficial 'belles lettres' humanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the great results of modern science within culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural knowledge must include 'what has been done by such men as Copernicus, Galileo, Newton, Darwin' — the great results of the modern scientific study of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining a person's cultural outfit, account for significant scientific achievements as essential content of modern culture, not only literary works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline of natural science: habit of dealing with facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of nature gives the 'habit of dealing with facts' through observation and experiment; natural knowledge is 'knowledge of things' rather than merely 'knowledge of words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value scientific training for educating attention to empirical evidence and experimental demonstration; this practical discipline is an important complement to literary study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance the claims of human powers in education
rubrics_metrics.description: Human life is built up by several powers: 'the power of conduct, the power of intellect and knowledge, the power of beauty, and the power of social life and manners' — education must meet and adjust the claims of them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let education be monopolized by either letters or sciences; assess curricula by how well they cultivate conduct, intellect, aesthetic sensibility, and social/moral life together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire to relate knowledge to conduct and beauty (role of letters)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is in most people a desire to 'relate pieces of knowledge to our sense for conduct, to our sense for beauty' — letters (humanities) help satisfy this integrative desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge educational programmes by whether they enable learners to connect factual knowledge to ethical and aesthetic understanding; letters play a distinct role in enabling such synthesis.
